newsitem.title: USA: Orange County regulatory troubles take new form.
newsitem.headline: Orange County regulatory troubles take new form.

text.p: Orange County's regulatory troubles may be far from over.

The Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) has subpoenaed municipal bond documents from the southern California county as part of its so-called "yield-burning" investigation, according to county records and officials.

Yield burning refers to allegations that bond underwriters overcharged states and other local governments in recent years for U.S. Treasury securities purchased in the open market to help refinance outstanding bonds.
The agency has over 20 yield-burning probes under way across the country, SEC officials have said.
Orange County, one of the wealthiest in the nation, filed for bankruptcy protection in December 1994 after sustaining losses estimated at more than $1.6 billion on risky investments.

The bankruptcy shocked Wall Street, and prompted both the SEC and the Internal Revenue Service to launch investigations into the crisis. The SEC settled with Orange County in January 1996. The IRS investigation continues.

The county has been trying to repair its image since emerging from bankruptcy one year ago. In June, top county officials met with Wall Street bankers and credit analysts in New York in hope of boosting confidence in the county.
The SEC's yield-burning investigation has, however, put the regulatory spotlight once again on Orange County.
Newly released county documents show that SEC investigators in Washington subpoenaed information from the county about a 1994 bond deal by the South Orange County Public Financing Authority.

The authority's $239 million bond deal, which refunded eight outstanding issues, was underwritten in August 1994 by PaineWebber Inc. and Stone & Youngberg LLC. Officials at both firms declined to comment.

The SEC subpoena was dated April 17 and, according to county documents, was issued as part of the agency's broad investigation of yield burning. County officials said they believe the yield-burning probe was in no way related to the county's bankruptcy crisis.
The county said it was cooperating fully with the SEC, and has sent the requested documents to the commission for review.
"We have yet to hear anything further from the SEC," county public finance manager Tom Beckett said.

Orange County officials said it was not clear what impact the commission's investigation would have on the 1994 bonds. If the SEC were to find that yield burning took place, the IRS could be drawn into the probe to determine whether the interest on the bonds should be taxable.
SEC officials were not immediately available to comment on the yield-burning probe. As a general rule, the SEC will neither confirm nor deny its investigations.
